skill.name: convex-explain-app
skill.description: Explain an existing Convex app — data model + relationships, public vs internal functions, auth/ownership model, components, a request→data flow — read from the schema and function surface. Read-only.
skill.summary: Map an existing Convex app's tables, functions, access rules, and request flows without changing the app.
skill.author: convex

finding_verdicts.reason: The inline Markdown names the functionSpec introspection surface. It contains no Ruby or shell invocation.
The backticks mark source paths and read-only MCP tool names. The workflow requests metadata through Convex MCP, not shell substitution.
The inline Markdown names the schema file and shows a Convex ID validator as an example. The workflow reads declarations without executing them.
The inline Markdown identifies a Convex package namespace. The instruction inventories existing integrations and environment variable references without requesting invocation or secret values.

content.value_statement: A Convex app's structure can be hard to understand when its behavior is spread across many files. This skill maps its tables, functions, access rules, and request flows without changing the app.
actual_capabilities: List tables and fields, identify ID relationships, and describe the access paths suggested by indexes.
Separate public and internal queries, mutations, and actions, and summarize what each function does and what it touches.
Describe how the app establishes identity and enforces ownership, and note when no authentication foundation is evident.
List configured components, HTTP routes, scheduled jobs, and external APIs referenced by actions.
Trace one or two representative requests from the caller through the backend to the data it reads or writes.
Use read-only Convex MCP metadata when a deployment is available, or inspect the source directly.
limitations: It describes authorization behavior but does not audit for security gaps.
It does not change source files, write app data, or deploy changes.
Without access to a deployment, it can explain local source but cannot verify the live function and table metadata.
It reports ambiguous behavior rather than guessing when the source does not show what happens.

use_cases.title: Get oriented in a Convex project
use_cases.description: See how tables relate and which functions clients can call before making a first contribution.

use_cases.title: Prepare an integration handoff
use_cases.description: Document HTTP routes, scheduled jobs, components, and external APIs for the team taking over the app.

use_cases.title: Document existing access rules
use_cases.description: Map identity setup and ownership checks before starting a separate authorization review.

prompt_templates.title: Get an app overview
prompt_templates.prompt: Explain this Convex app using the local source. Start with table relationships and the difference between public and internal functions.
prompt_templates.scenario: First look at an unfamiliar repository.

prompt_templates.title: Map identity and ownership
prompt_templates.prompt: Explain how this app identifies callers and checks ownership. Name the fields and checks you find, and flag anything the source does not establish.
prompt_templates.scenario: Documenting how access is intended to work.

prompt_templates.title: Trace a feature
prompt_templates.prompt: Trace the task creation and listing flows if they exist. Identify the functions, ownership checks, tables, and indexes involved in each flow.
prompt_templates.scenario: Preparing to change a feature with linked data.

prompt_templates.title: Map a deployed backend
prompt_templates.prompt: Use read-only Convex MCP metadata for the target deployment if available. Explain the function surface, data model, HTTP routes, scheduled jobs, and external integrations. Mark what you could verify only in source.
prompt_templates.scenario: Preparing a handoff for a deployed app.

output_examples.input: Explain the tables and task functions in this project tracker.
output: Each task belongs to a project and has a user as its owner.
The public task list query uses the owner index to return only the signed-in user's tasks.
The reminder sender is an internal action that clients cannot call directly.

output_examples.input: Trace how a reminder reaches the email provider.
output: A scheduled job starts an internal action that reads tasks due for reminders.
The action sends each reminder through the configured email provider.
The source identifies the environment variable for the provider credential, but does not show its value.

best_practices: Name the target deployment if you want live metadata, so the explanation uses the intended environment.
Identify a feature or entry point when you need a focused request trace.
Use the architecture map as input to a separate security review before making changes to access rules.
anti_patterns: Treating a local source description as proof of what is deployed.
Assuming a public function has no access checks just because clients can call it.
Using the skill to request code changes, data writes, or deployment operations.

faq.question: Do I need a running deployment?
faq.answer: No. The skill can inspect the local Convex source when a deployment is not available.

faq.question: Does this skill modify my app?
faq.answer: No. It reads source or deployment metadata and produces an explanation.

faq.question: Can it tell me which functions clients can call?
faq.answer: Yes. It separates public functions from internal functions and summarizes the role of each.

faq.question: Does it check for authorization vulnerabilities?
faq.answer: No. It describes the identity and ownership model. Use a separate security review to assess whether the checks are sufficient.

faq.question: Which integrations does it document?
faq.answer: It lists configured Convex components, HTTP routes, scheduled jobs, and external APIs referenced by actions.

faq.question: What happens when the code is unclear?
faq.answer: The skill identifies what the available source or metadata does not establish instead of inventing behavior.
